patient.chief_complaint: Progressive word-finding difficulty and personality change over 2 months
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jerome Harris is a 47-year-old right-handed man and high school English teacher who presents with a 2-month history of progressive cognitive and behavioral changes, initially attributed to stress and worsening depression. His husband first noticed something was wrong approximately 8 weeks ago when he began struggling to find words during conversations, occasionally substituting incorrect words or trailing off mid-sentence. As an English teacher, his vocabulary had always been exceptional, and these lapses were immediately noticeable to family and colleagues. Over the following weeks, he became increasingly irritable and short-tempered, which was uncharacteristic. He snapped at students in class on several occasions and had two arguments with colleagues over trivial matters, prompting the principal to suggest he take a leave of absence. His husband also reports that he has become somewhat apathetic, losing interest in reading novels — previously his greatest passion — and spending hours staring at the television without engaging with the content. Approximately 6 weeks ago, he began complaining of dull, pressure-like headaches, predominantly on the left side, that were worse in the morning and would gradually improve over the course of the day. The headaches were initially responsive to ibuprofen but have become more persistent over the past 3 weeks. Three weeks ago, he had an episode where his right hand began shaking involuntarily for approximately 30 seconds while he was eating breakfast. He did not lose consciousness but felt confused for several minutes afterward. His husband witnessed the episode and described rhythmic jerking of the right hand that he could not suppress. He was evaluated by his primary care physician, who increased his sertraline dose, suspecting worsening depression. However, his symptoms continued to progress, and he was referred to neurology. At the outpatient neurology visit one week ago, the examining neurologist was concerned by his word-finding difficulty and subtle left-sided motor findings, and ordered an urgent MRI of the brain. The MRI revealed a left temporal lobe lesion, and he was admitted for further workup. The patient himself acknowledges feeling 'not right' but minimizes the extent of his symptoms. He attributes his personality changes to stress at work and denies feeling depressed, though he admits he has been sleeping more than usual and has lost approximately 4 kg over the past two months without trying.

mri.impression: Irregular heterogeneously enhancing left temporal mass with infiltrative margins, surrounding vasogenic edema, and mild mass effect. The lesion is centered in the superior and middle temporal gyri with extension to the insular cortex. The enhancement pattern is thick and nodular rather than a classic ring, and the infiltrative margins raise concern for high-grade glioma. The absence of classic central necrosis and ring enhancement makes this somewhat atypical for glioblastoma, though the heterogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion at margins, and infiltrative behavior favor a high-grade astrocytic neoplasm. Differential considerations include anaplastic astrocytoma (WHO grade 3) versus glioblastoma (WHO grade 4). Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Stupp Protocol: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.relevance: Landmark trial establishing standard of care: maximal safe resection followed by concurrent chemoradiation (60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2) followed by 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2 days 1-5 of 28-day cycle)

results.title: MGMT promoter methylation status and temozolomide benefit in glioblastoma
results.relevance: MGMT unmethylated patients derive less benefit from temozolomide but still receive it as standard of care; median survival approximately 12-14 months vs 21 months for methylated

results.title: Tumor treating fields (TTFields) for newly diagnosed glioblastoma
results.relevance: TTFields added to maintenance temozolomide improved median overall survival to 20.9 months vs 16 months; FDA-approved addition to standard of care

output.summary: Standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype is the Stupp protocol: maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent chemoradiation (60 Gy with temozolomide) and adjuvant temozolomide. For MGMT-unmethylated tumors, the benefit of temozolomide is reduced but it remains part of standard therapy. Tumor treating fields (TTFields/Optune) are an FDA-approved addition to maintenance therapy. Clinical trial enrollment should be considered, particularly for MGMT-unmethylated tumors. Bevacizumab may be considered at recurrence. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: Indistinguishable on imaging alone; molecular and histologic features differentiate
No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against

Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging mass effect (effacement of ventricles / sulci / cisterns): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization (mass, edema, eloquent-cortex proximity) is standard of care before neurosurgical tissue acquisition

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to control symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of intracranial mass effect — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a left temporal lobe heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Mass effect, even when modest, makes lumbar puncture risky and low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis — MRI must precede any consideration of LP
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
